newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea to enact law banning money laundering.
newsitem.headline: South Korea to enact law banning money laundering.

text.p: South Korea's finance minister said on Tuesday the government would push legislation banning money laundering to prevent corruption and accumulation of slush funds.
Minister Kang Kyong-shik also said his ministry would exempt small companies from probes into funding sources.
He said funds used for the launching and the capital increase of small firms and venture companies would not be tracked.
These steps were part of a package that the finance ministry disclosed to improve the real-name financial system, which bans the use of false names in all financial transactions.
The system was introduced in 1993 to root out corruption and force underground money into the economic system.
Minister Kang said his ministry would not investigate the source of money if it is reported to tax authorities and deposited into real-name accounts.
Currently, financial authorities are required to investigate bank account holders who move more than 200 million won into a real-name account from a false-name account.

"We plan to complete the legislation of the revision as early as possible, even before the regular session of the National Assembly," Kang said. Kang also said the revision would be carried out in a way not to destroy the basic principle of the real-name financial system.
The plenary session usually opens in September.
Ministry officials said the ministry was not considering allowing false-name trading of long-term bonds issued to raise funds for infrastructure projects, as had been rumoured in the stock market.
"Such bond trading is unlikely because that means the complete surrender to the old practice of dubious financial transactions," said a ministry official.
On Monday, President Kim Young-sam urged Kang to leave intact the basic principles of the financial transaction system.
When Kang was appointed new minister earlier this month, he told reporters he would review the real-name system, which is widely believed to have caused bottlenecks in the economy.
